And shutting out every doubt, he would go to the law courts, fall into conversation with his colleagues, and settle into his chair with the old careless ease, scanning the crowd with a thoughtful look and resting both his wasted arms on the oak armrests; he would lean over to a colleague as usual and draw his papers closer and trade whispers with him, and then suddenly look up, sit straight, say the appointed words, and open the session. But right in the middle of the proceedings the pain in his side, indifferent to whatever stage the case had reached, would start up its own gnawing work. Ivan Ilyich would turn his mind to it and try to drive the thought of it off, but it was no use. It would come and stand before him and stare at him, and he would freeze, the light would go out of his eyes, and he would start asking himself all over again whether It was the only thing that was real. And his colleagues and subordinates would watch, surprised and dismayed, as this brilliant, sharp-witted judge grew muddled and made mistakes. He would shake himself, struggle to gather his wits, somehow get the session to its close, and go home with the wretched knowledge that his work could no longer do what it had always done for him: hide from him what he wanted hidden, and rescue him from It. And the worst of it was that It drew his attention not so that he would do something about it, but only so that he would look at It, look it straight in the face: look at it and, without being able to do a single thing, suffer beyond all words.

To escape this state Ivan Ilyich went looking for comforts, for new screens, and new screens were found and seemed to save him for a while, but then they would fall apart at once, or rather turn transparent, as though It passed right through them and nothing could veil It.

In those last days he would walk into the drawing room he had arranged himself, the very drawing room where he had taken his fall and for the sake of which, how bitterly absurd it seemed now, he had thrown his life away, since he knew his illness had begun with that knock. He would come in and notice that something had scratched the polished surface of the table. He would hunt for the cause and discover it was the bronze trim of an album that had gotten bent. He would pick up the expensive album he had so lovingly put together and feel annoyed at his daughter and her friends for their carelessness, since the album was torn in places and some of the photographs were upside down. He would carefully set it right and bend the bronze back into shape. Then it would strike him that all of these things should be moved to another corner of the room, over by the plants. He would call the footman, but his daughter or his wife would come to help, and they would disagree, and his wife would contradict him, and he would argue and lose his temper. But that was fine, because then he was not thinking about It. It was out of sight.

But then, when he was shifting something himself, his wife would say, "Let the servants do it. You'll hurt yourself again." And suddenly It would flash through the screen, and he would see it. Just a flash, and he would hope it would vanish, but he could not help paying attention to his side. "It's sitting there just like before, gnawing away." And now he could no longer forget It; he could see it plainly, watching him from behind the flowers. "What is all this for?" "It really is true. I lost my life over that curtain, as if I'd fallen storming a fortress. Is that possible? How horrible, how stupid. It can't be true. It can't be, and yet it is." He would go into his study, lie down, and once again be alone with It, face to face with It. And there was nothing to be done with It except to look at it and shudder.

chapters.title: Chapter 7
paragraphs: How it came about is impossible to say, because it happened gradually, step by step, without anyone noticing, but by the third month of Ivan Ilyich's illness his wife, his daughter, his son, his acquaintances, the doctors, the servants, and above all he himself were aware that the only thing about him that interested other people was how soon he would vacate his place, free the living at last from the awkwardness of his presence, and be freed himself from his suffering. He slept less and less. They gave him opium and injected him with morphine, but it brought no relief. The dull haze he felt in his half-asleep state was a little soothing at first, but only because it was new; before long it became just as distressing as the pain, and then even worse.

Special meals were prepared for him on the doctors' orders, but every one of them tasted more tasteless and revolting than the last. Special arrangements had to be made for his bodily functions too, and each time it was an ordeal for him, an ordeal of filth and indecency and stench, and of knowing that another person had to take part in it.

And yet it was precisely through this most degrading business that Ivan Ilyich found some comfort. Gerasim, the butler's young assistant, always came in to carry the things out. Gerasim was a clean, healthy young peasant, grown stout on town food, always cheerful and bright. At first it embarrassed Ivan Ilyich to see him, in his clean Russian peasant clothes, doing such a disgusting task.

Once, having gotten up from the commode too weak to pull his trousers up, he dropped into a soft armchair and stared in horror at his bare, withered thighs, with the muscles standing out so sharply on them. Gerasim came in with a firm, light tread, his heavy boots giving off a pleasant smell of tar and fresh winter air, wearing a clean canvas apron, the sleeves of his cotton shirt rolled up over his strong, bare young arms; and keeping his eyes off his sick master out of consideration for his feelings, holding back the joy of life that shone out of his face, he went over to the commode.
"Gerasim," said Ivan Ilyich in a weak voice.
Gerasim flinched, plainly afraid he had done something wrong, and with a quick motion turned his fresh, kind, simple young face, which had just begun to show the first soft signs of a beard.
"Yes, sir?"
"This must be very unpleasant for you. You'll have to forgive me. I'm helpless."
"Why, not at all, sir," said Gerasim, his eyes lighting up and his bright white teeth showing. "What's a little trouble? You're a sick man, sir."

And his quick, strong hands did their familiar work, and he left the room, stepping lightly. Five minutes later he came back, just as lightly. Ivan Ilyich was still sitting where he had been, in the armchair. "Gerasim," he said when the young man had put the freshly washed pot back in place. "Come here, please, and help me." Gerasim came over. "Lift me up. It's hard for me to get up on my own, and I've sent Dmitri away."

Gerasim went to him, took hold of his master with his strong arms, deftly but gently, in the same way that he walked, lifted him, supported him with one hand, and with the other pulled up his trousers, and would have set him back down, but Ivan Ilyich asked to be helped over to the sofa. Without any apparent effort or strain, Gerasim led him, all but carrying him, to the sofa and settled him on it. "Thank you. How easily and well you do everything."
Gerasim smiled again and turned to go. But Ivan Ilyich found his presence such a comfort that he did not want to let him leave.
"One more thing, please. Move that chair over. No, the other one, under my feet. It's easier for me with my feet raised."
Gerasim brought the chair, set it down gently in place, and lifted Ivan Ilyich's legs onto it. It seemed to Ivan Ilyich that he felt better while Gerasim was holding his legs up.
"It's better when my legs are higher," he said. "Put that cushion under them."
Gerasim did so. He lifted the legs again and placed them, and again Ivan Ilyich felt better while Gerasim held his legs. When he set them down, Ivan Ilyich thought he felt worse.
"Gerasim," he said. "Are you busy just now?"
"Not at all, sir," said Gerasim, who had learned from the townspeople how to talk to gentlefolk.
"What still needs doing?"
"What needs doing? I've done everything except chop the wood for tomorrow."
"Then hold my legs up a little higher, would you?"
"Of course I can. Why not?" And Gerasim raised his master's legs higher, and Ivan Ilyich felt that in that position he had no pain at all.
"And what about the wood?"
"Don't you worry about that, sir. There's plenty of time."
Ivan Ilyich told Gerasim to sit down and keep holding his legs, and he began to talk with him. And strange to say, it seemed to him that he felt better while Gerasim held his legs up.

After that Ivan Ilyich would sometimes call Gerasim and have him hold his legs up on his shoulders, and he liked talking with him. Gerasim did it all easily, willingly, simply, and with a kindness that moved Ivan Ilyich. Health, strength, and vitality in other people offended him, but Gerasim's strength and vitality did not wound him; they soothed him.

What tormented Ivan Ilyich most was the lie, the deception that, for some reason, everyone went along with, that he was not dying but only ill, and that if he just stayed calm and followed the treatment, something very good would come of it. He knew that whatever they did, nothing would come of it but more excruciating suffering and death. And the lie tortured him, their refusal to admit what they all knew and what he knew, their determination to lie to him about his terrible state and to make him take part in the lie. These lies, performed over him on the eve of his death, lies meant to drag this awful, solemn event down to the level of their social calls, their curtains, their sturgeon at dinner, were a terrible agony for Ivan Ilyich. And, strangely enough, many times while they were going through their performance over him, he came within a hair of crying out to them, "Stop lying! You know and I know that I'm dying. So at least stop lying about it!" But he never had the nerve to do it. The terrible, dreadful act of his dying was, he could see, reduced by everyone around him to the level of some chance unpleasantness, almost a breach of manners, as if someone had walked into a drawing room trailing a bad smell, and this was done by the very decorum he had served his whole life. He saw that no one felt for him, because no one even wanted to grasp his situation. Only Gerasim understood it and pitied him. And so Ivan Ilyich felt at ease only with him. He felt comforted when Gerasim held up his legs, sometimes all night long, and refused to go to bed, saying, "Don't you worry, Ivan Ilyich, I'll get plenty of sleep later," or when he suddenly grew familiar and said, "It would be different if you weren't sick, but as things are, why should I begrudge a little trouble?" Gerasim alone did not lie; everything about him showed that he alone understood how matters really stood and saw no need to hide it, and simply pitied his wasted, failing master. Once, when Ivan Ilyich was sending him away, he even said it outright: "We're all going to die, so why should I begrudge a little trouble?" By which he meant that he did not find the work a burden, because he was doing it for a dying man and hoped that someone would do the same for him when his time came.

Apart from this lying, or perhaps because of it, what tormented Ivan Ilyich most was that no one pitied him the way he longed to be pitied. At certain moments, after long bouts of suffering, what he wanted more than anything, though he would have been ashamed to admit it, was for someone to pity him the way you pity a sick child. He longed to be held and soothed and wept over. He knew he was an important official, that his beard was going gray, and that therefore what he wanted was impossible, but he longed for it all the same. And in the way Gerasim treated him there was something close to what he wanted, and so it comforted him. Ivan Ilyich wanted to cry, wanted to be held and wept over, and then his colleague Shebek would arrive, and instead of weeping and being comforted Ivan Ilyich would put on a grave, severe, thoughtful air and, out of sheer habit, would offer his opinion on some ruling of the Court of Cassation and dig in stubbornly to defend it. This falseness around him and inside him poisoned his last days more than anything else.

chapters.title: Chapter 8
paragraphs: It was morning. He knew it was morning because Gerasim had gone and Peter the footman had come in, snuffed out the candles, drawn back one of the curtains, and begun quietly tidying up. Whether it was morning or evening, Friday or Sunday, made no difference; it was all exactly the same: the gnawing, relentless, agonizing pain that never let up for an instant, the awareness of a life draining away inexorably but not yet gone, the approach of that dreaded, hateful Death that was the only reality, and always the same falseness. What did days, weeks, or hours matter in a state like that?
"Would you like some tea, sir?"
"He wants everything done on schedule, and he wants the gentlefolk to have their tea in the morning," thought Ivan Ilyich, and only said, "No."
"Wouldn't you like to move to the sofa, sir?"
"He wants to tidy the room, and I'm in his way. I'm filth and disorder," he thought, and only said,
"No, leave me alone."
The man kept bustling about. Ivan Ilyich stretched out his hand. Peter came over, ready to help.
"What is it, sir?"
"My watch."
Peter picked up the watch, which was lying close by, and handed it to his master.
"Half past eight. Are they up?"
"No, sir, except Vladimir Ivanovich, who has gone off to school. Praskovya Fedorovna asked me to wake her if you wanted her. Shall I?"
"No, no need." "Maybe I should have some tea after all," he thought, and added aloud, "Yes, bring me some tea."

Peter started for the door, but Ivan Ilyich dreaded being left alone. "How can I keep him here? Oh yes, my medicine." "Peter, give me my medicine." "Why not? Maybe it can still do some good." He took a spoonful and swallowed it. "No, it won't help. It's all nonsense, all a fraud," he decided the moment he tasted that familiar, sickly, hopeless taste. "No, I can't believe in it anymore. But the pain, why this pain? If only it would stop, just for a moment." And he groaned. Peter turned toward him. "It's all right. Go and fetch the tea."

Peter went out. Alone, Ivan Ilyich groaned, not so much from the pain, terrible as it was, as from the anguish in his mind. Always and forever the same, always these endless days and nights. If only it would come faster. If only what would come faster? Death, darkness? No, no! Anything but death!

When Peter came back with the tea on a tray, Ivan Ilyich stared at him for a while in confusion, not understanding who he was or what he was. The stare unsettled Peter, and his discomfort brought Ivan Ilyich back to himself.
"Oh, the tea. Good, set it down. Just help me wash and put on a clean shirt."

And Ivan Ilyich began to wash. Resting between each step, he washed his hands and then his face, brushed his teeth, combed his hair, and looked in the mirror. He was horrified by what he saw, above all by the limp way his hair lay against his pale forehead.

While his shirt was being changed he knew he would be even more frightened by the sight of his body, so he avoided looking at it. At last he was ready. He pulled on a dressing gown, wrapped himself in a plaid blanket, and sat down in the armchair to have his tea. For a moment he felt refreshed, but the instant he began to drink the tea he tasted that same taste again, and the pain came back too. He forced himself to finish it, then lay down, stretched out his legs, and sent Peter away. Always the same. Now a spark of hope flares up, then a sea of despair surges over him, and always the pain; always the pain, always the despair, and always the same. Alone, he felt a dreadful, desperate urge to call someone, yet he knew in advance that with others around it would only be worse. "Another dose of morphine, to black out. I'll tell him, the doctor, that he has to think of something else. This is impossible, impossible, I can't go on like this."

An hour goes by like that, and another. But now the doorbell rings. Maybe it's the doctor. It is. In he comes, fresh, hearty, plump, and cheerful, with a look on his face that seems to say, "Now, now, you're in a panic about something, but we'll soon set it all right for you." The doctor knows perfectly well that this expression is out of place here, but he has put it on once and for all and can't take it off, like a man who has dressed in a frock coat in the morning to go around paying calls. The doctor rubs his hands briskly and reassuringly.
"Brr! It's cold out there! Such a sharp frost; just let me warm up a bit," he says, as if it were only a matter of waiting until he was warm, and then he would put everything right.
"Well now, how are you?"

Ivan Ilyich feels that the doctor would like to say, "Well, how are things with us?" but that even he senses this won't do, and so he says instead, "How was your night?" Ivan Ilyich looks at him as if to say, "Are you really never ashamed of lying?" But the doctor has no wish to understand the question, and Ivan Ilyich says, "Just as terrible as ever. The pain never leaves me, never lets up. If only there were something..."

"Yes, you sick people are always like that. There, now I think I'm warm enough. Even Praskovya Fedorovna, who's so particular, couldn't fault my temperature. Well, now I can say good morning," and the doctor shakes his patient's hand.

Then, dropping the earlier playfulness, he sets a very serious face and begins to examine the patient, taking his pulse and his temperature, and then comes the tapping and the listening. Ivan Ilyich knows clearly and for certain that all of this is nonsense and pure deception, but when the doctor gets down on one knee and leans over him, putting his ear first higher then lower and going through various gymnastics over him with a meaningful look on his face, Ivan Ilyich submits to it all, just as he used to submit to the lawyers' speeches even though he knew very well that they were all lying and exactly why they were lying.
The doctor, kneeling on the sofa, is still tapping away when Praskovya Fedorovna's silk dress rustles at the door and she is heard scolding Peter for not having told her the doctor had arrived.

She comes in, kisses her husband, and immediately sets about proving that she has been up for ages and that only a misunderstanding kept her from being there when the doctor arrived. Ivan Ilyich looks at her, takes her in from head to foot, and holds against her the whiteness and plumpness and cleanness of her hands and neck, the gloss of her hair, the sparkle of her lively eyes. He hates her with his whole soul. And the surge of hatred he feels for her makes her very touch agony to him.

Her attitude toward him and his illness is still the same. Just as the doctor had taken up a certain stance toward his patient that he could not now drop, so she had taken one toward him, that he was failing to do something he ought to do and had only himself to blame, and that she reproached him for it out of love, and she could not change that stance now either.
"You see, he doesn't listen to me and won't take his medicine on time. And worst of all, he lies in a position that's surely bad for him, with his legs up."
She described how he made Gerasim hold his legs up.
The doctor gave a smile of condescending kindness that said, "What can you do? These sick people get foolish notions like that, but we have to forgive them."

When the examination was over, the doctor looked at his watch, and then Praskovya Fedorovna informed Ivan Ilyich that of course it was up to him, but she had sent today for a famous specialist, who would examine him and consult with Michael Danilovich.

"Now please don't make a fuss. I'm doing this for my own sake," she said with irony, making it clear that she was doing it all for his sake and only said this so as to leave him no grounds to refuse. He stayed silent, frowning. He felt himself caught in such a tangle of falsehood that it was hard to make out anything at all.

Everything she did for him she did entirely for herself, and she told him she was doing for herself what she was in fact doing for herself, as if this were so unbelievable that he was bound to understand it to mean the opposite.

At half past eleven the famous specialist arrived. Again came the tapping and the weighty conversations, in front of him and in the next room, about the kidneys and the appendix, the questions and answers, all delivered with such an air of importance that once more, in place of the real question of life and death that now alone faced him, up came the question of the kidney and the appendix, which were not behaving as they should and would now be set upon by Michael Danilovich and the specialist and forced to mend their ways.

The famous specialist took his leave with a serious but not hopeless look, and when Ivan Ilyich, his eyes shining with fear and hope, put the timid question of whether there was any chance of recovery, the specialist said he could not promise anything, but there was a possibility. The look of hope with which Ivan Ilyich watched the doctor go out was so pitiful that Praskovya Fedorovna, seeing it, actually wept as she left the room to hand the doctor his fee.

The lift in spirits brought on by the doctor's encouragement did not last long. The same room, the same pictures, curtains, wallpaper, medicine bottles were all still there, and the same aching, suffering body, and Ivan Ilyich began to moan. They gave him a subcutaneous injection and he sank into oblivion.
It was twilight when he came around. They brought him his dinner and he managed with difficulty to swallow some beef broth, and then everything was the same again, and night was coming on.

After dinner, at seven o'clock, Praskovya Fedorovna came into the room in evening dress, her full bosom pushed up by her corset, traces of powder on her face. She had reminded him that morning that they were going to the theater. Sarah Bernhardt was in town and they had a box, which he himself had insisted they take. Now he had forgotten all about it, and her get-up offended him, but he hid his irritation when he remembered that he had been the one who insisted they get the box and go, because it would be an instructive and aesthetic treat for the children.

Praskovya Fedorovna came in pleased with herself, but with a slightly guilty air. She sat down and asked how he was, but, as he could tell, only for the sake of asking and not because she wanted to know, since she knew there was nothing to learn, and then went on to what she really wanted to say: that she would not have gone for anything, but the box had already been taken, and Helen and their daughter were going, along with Petrishchev (the examining magistrate, their daughter's fiancé), and that it was out of the question to let them go on their own; but that she would so much rather sit a while with him; and that he must be sure to follow the doctor's orders while she was out.
"Oh, and Fedor Petrovich" (the fiancé) "would like to look in. May he? And Lisa?"
"All right."

Their daughter came in in full evening dress, her fresh young flesh on display (flaunting the very flesh that in his own case caused so much suffering), strong, healthy, plainly in love, and impatient with illness, suffering, and death, because they got in the way of her happiness.

Fedor Petrovich came in too, in evening dress, his hair curled à la Capoul, a tight stiff collar around his long sinewy neck, an enormous white shirtfront, and narrow black trousers stretched tight over his strong thighs. He had one white glove pulled tight onto his hand and was holding his opera hat.

Behind him the schoolboy slipped in unnoticed, in a new uniform, the poor little fellow, and wearing gloves. There were terribly dark shadows under his eyes, and Ivan Ilyich knew exactly what they meant. His son had always struck him as a pitiful figure, and now it was dreadful to see the boy's frightened look of pity. It seemed to Ivan Ilyich that, besides Gerasim, Vasya was the only one who understood and pitied him.

They all sat down and again asked how he was. A silence followed. Lisa asked her mother about the opera glasses, and there was a squabble between mother and daughter over who had taken them and where they had been put. It left an unpleasant feeling in the air.

Fedor Petrovich asked Ivan Ilyich whether he had ever seen Sarah Bernhardt. At first Ivan Ilyich did not catch the question, but then he answered, "No. Have you seen her before?" "Yes, in Adrienne Lecouvreur."

Praskovya Fedorovna named a few roles in which Sarah Bernhardt was especially good. Her daughter disagreed. A conversation sprang up about the elegance and realism of her acting, the sort of conversation that gets repeated again and again and is always the same.

In the middle of the conversation Fedor Petrovich glanced at Ivan Ilyich and fell silent. The others looked at him too and grew silent. Ivan Ilyich was staring straight ahead with glittering eyes, plainly furious with them. Something had to be done to put it right, but it was impossible. The silence had to be broken, but for a while no one dared, and they all grew afraid that the polite pretense would suddenly collapse and the truth would become clear to everyone. Lisa was the first to find the courage to break the silence, but in trying to hide what they were all feeling, she gave it away.

"Well, if we're going, it's time we started," she said, glancing at her watch, a present from her father, and giving Fedor Petrovich a faint, knowing smile about something only the two of them shared. She got up with a rustle of her dress. They all rose, said goodnight, and left.

When they had gone, Ivan Ilyich felt that he was better; the falseness had gone out with them. But the pain stayed, that same pain and that same fear that made everything monotonously the same, nothing harder and nothing easier. Everything was worse.

Again minute followed minute and hour followed hour. Everything stayed the same and there was no end to it. And the unavoidable end of it all grew more and more terrible. "Yes, send Gerasim in," he answered a question Peter had asked.

chapters.title: Chapter 9
paragraphs: His wife came home late that night. She crept in on tiptoe, but he heard her anyway, opened his eyes, and quickly shut them again. She wanted to send Gerasim off and sit up with him herself, but he opened his eyes and said, "No, go away."
"Are you in a lot of pain?"
"The same as always."
"Take some opium."
He gave in and took it. She left.

Until around three in the morning he lay in a dull, dazed misery. He felt as though he and his pain were being shoved into a narrow, deep black sack, pushed in further and further, yet never quite reaching the bottom. The whole thing was horrible enough on its own, and on top of it came the suffering. He was terrified, and yet he longed to drop all the way through the sack; he fought against it, and yet he was helping it along. Then all at once he tore through, fell, and came back to himself. Gerasim was sitting at the foot of the bed, dozing in quiet patience, while Ivan Ilych lay there with his thin, stockinged legs propped on Gerasim's shoulders. The same shaded candle was burning, and the same pain went on without a break.
"Go away, Gerasim," he whispered.
"It's no trouble, sir. I'll stay a bit longer."
"No. Go."

He lifted his legs off Gerasim's shoulders, rolled onto his side with his head on his arm, and was filled with pity for himself. He only waited until Gerasim had gone into the next room, and then he held back no longer and cried like a child. He wept for his own helplessness, for his terrible loneliness, for the cruelty of people, for the cruelty of God, and for the fact that there seemed to be no God at all. "Why have You done all this? Why have You brought me here? Why, why do You torture me like this?"

He did not expect any answer, and he wept precisely because there was no answer and never could be one. The pain flared up sharper again, but he did not move and did not call out. He told himself, "Go ahead, then. Strike me! But what for? What have I done to You? What is it all for?"

Then he went still. He not only stopped crying, he even held his breath and listened with his whole being. It was as if he were listening, not to a voice he could hear, but to the voice of his own soul, to the stream of thoughts rising up inside him.
"What is it you want?" That was the first clear thought he made out, the first he could put into words. "What do you want? What do you want?" he kept repeating to himself.
"What do I want? To live, and not to suffer," he answered.
And again he listened so intently that even the pain could not pull him away. "To live? Live how?" his inner voice asked.
"Why, to live the way I used to—comfortably and pleasantly."
"The way you lived before, comfortably and pleasantly?" the voice repeated.

And in his mind he started running back through the best moments of that pleasant life. But the strange thing was that none of those supposedly best moments looked anything like what they had seemed at the time—none of them, except his very earliest memories of childhood. Back there, in childhood, there had been something genuinely good, something he could live on if it could only come back. But the child who had known that happiness no longer existed; it was like remembering a stranger.

The moment he reached the period that had shaped the present Ivan Ilych, everything that had then looked like joy dissolved before his eyes and turned into something petty, and often something repugnant.

And the further he moved from childhood and the closer he came to the present, the more worthless and questionable those joys became. It started with the School of Law. A little real good could still be found there—there was lightheartedness, friendship, and hope. But in the senior years even those good moments had grown scarcer. Then, in the early years of his official career, when he served under the governor, some pleasant moments came again—memories of being in love with a woman. After that it all blurred, and the good thinned out further still; and the further on he went, the less of it there was. His marriage, which had really been an accident, then the disappointment that followed, his wife's bad breath, the sensuality and the pretending; then that deadly grind of official life and all those worries about money, a year of it, then two, then ten, then twenty—and always the same thing. And the longer it lasted, the deader it grew. "It's as though I'd been walking steadily downhill while I believed I was climbing. That's exactly what happened. In the eyes of the world I was rising, and at the very same rate life was draining out of me. And now it's all finished, and there's nothing left but death.

"So what does it mean? Why? It can't be that life is this senseless and this hideous. But if it really has been so hideous and senseless, why must I die, and die in such agony? Something is wrong here. Maybe I didn't live the way I should have," the thought suddenly came to him. "But how can that be, when I did everything properly?" he answered himself, and at once pushed away from his mind this one solution to all the riddles of life and death, dismissing it as utterly out of the question.

"Then what is it you want now? To live? Live how? Live the way you lived in the courtroom, when the usher cried out, 'The judge is coming!' The judge is coming, the judge!" he said to himself. "Here he is, the judge. But I'm not guilty!" he burst out angrily. "What is it for?" He stopped crying, turned his face to the wall, and kept turning the same question over and over: why, and to what end, was all this horror? But however hard he thought, he found no answer. And whenever it crossed his mind, as it often did, that all of it came from his not having lived the way he should have, he immediately called up the whole correctness of his life and dismissed so peculiar an idea.

chapters.title: Chapter 10
paragraphs: Another two weeks went by. Ivan Ilych no longer got up from his sofa. He refused to lie in bed and stayed on the sofa instead, facing the wall almost the whole time. He suffered the same unbroken agony, and in his loneliness he kept circling the same unanswerable question: "What is this? Can it really be Death?" And the voice inside him answered, "Yes, it is Death."
"Why all this suffering?" And the voice answered, "For no reason. It just is." Past that, and apart from that, there was nothing.

From the very start of his illness, from his first visit to the doctor, Ivan Ilych's life had swung between two opposite moods that took turns: now despair and the dread of this incomprehensible, terrible death, and now hope and a keenly interested study of how his body was working. One moment all he saw before him was a kidney or an intestine that had temporarily shirked its job, and the next moment all he saw was that incomprehensible, dreadful death there was no escaping.

These two states of mind had alternated from the beginning of his illness, but as it advanced, the idea of the kidney grew more doubtful and far-fetched, while the sense of approaching death grew more real.

He only had to recall what he had been three months earlier and what he was now, to recall how steadily he had been sliding downhill, and every chance of hope was shattered. Lately, in the loneliness that gripped him as he lay facing the back of the sofa—a loneliness in the middle of a crowded city, surrounded by countless acquaintances and relatives, and yet as complete as any he could have known at the bottom of the sea or buried underground—in that terrible loneliness Ivan Ilych had lived only in memories of the past. Scenes from his past kept rising before him one after another. They always began with whatever was nearest in time and then traveled back to what was most remote—to his childhood—and settled there. If he thought of the stewed prunes he had been offered that day, his mind would go back to the raw, wrinkled French plums of his childhood, their odd flavor, the rush of saliva when he sucked the stones, and along with that taste came a whole train of memories from those days—his nurse, his brother, their toys. "No, I mustn't think about that. It's too painful," Ivan Ilych would say to himself, and drag himself back to the present—to the button on the back of the sofa and the creases in the morocco leather. "Morocco is expensive, but it doesn't hold up well. There was a quarrel about it. But it was a different quarrel and a different bit of morocco that time we tore father's portfolio and got punished, and mamma brought us tarts..." And again his thoughts dwelt on his childhood, and again it hurt, and he tried to drive the memories off and fasten his mind on something else.

Then, alongside that chain of memories, another series would run through his mind—the way his illness had advanced and grown worse. There too, the further back he looked, the more life there had been. There had been more goodness in his life, and more life itself. The two streams flowed together. "Just as the pain has gone on getting worse and worse, so my whole life has gotten worse and worse," he thought. "There's one bright spot back there at the very beginning of life, and after that everything turns blacker and blacker and rushes faster and faster—in inverse proportion to the square of the distance from death," Ivan Ilych thought. And the image of a stone falling, gathering speed as it goes, came into his mind. Life, a series of mounting agonies, hurtles faster and faster toward its end—the most terrible agony of all. "I'm falling..." He shuddered, shifted his body, and tried to fight it off, but he already knew that there was no fighting it, and again, with eyes worn out from staring yet unable to stop seeing what was in front of them, he stared at the back of the sofa and waited—waited for that dreadful drop, that crash, that destruction.

"There's no resisting it," he said to himself. "If only I could understand what it's all for. But that's impossible too. There would be an explanation if you could say I hadn't lived the way I should have. But there's no saying that," and he recalled all the legality, the correctness, the propriety of his life. "That, at least, certainly can't be admitted," he thought, and his lips curved into an ironic smile, as if someone could see that smile and be fooled by it. "There's no explanation! Agony, death... What for?"

chapters.title: Chapter 11
paragraphs: Another two weeks passed in this way, and during that fortnight something happened that Ivan Ilych and his wife had been hoping for: Petrishchev formally proposed. It came in the evening. The next day Praskovya Fyodorovna walked into her husband's room, working out how best to break the news to him—but during that very night his condition had taken a fresh turn for the worse. She found him still on the sofa, but lying differently. He was on his back, groaning and staring straight ahead with a fixed gaze.
She started to remind him about his medicines, but he turned his eyes on her with such a look that she did not finish the sentence; the look was so full of hatred, and aimed at her in particular.
"For Christ's sake, let me die in peace," he said.

She would have left, but just then their daughter came in and went over to say good morning. He looked at her the same way he had looked at his wife, and when she asked how he was feeling, he said curtly that he would soon rid them all of himself. The two of them said nothing, sat with him a little while, and then went out.
"How is it our fault?" Lisa said to her mother. "As if we'd done something! I feel sorry for papa, but why should we be put through this?"

The doctor came at his usual hour. Ivan Ilych answered him with "Yes" and "No," never taking his angry eyes off the man, and finally said, "You know perfectly well you can't do anything for me, so leave me alone."
"We can ease your suffering."
"You can't even do that. Let me be."

The doctor went out to the drawing room and told Praskovya Fyodorovna that the case was very grave, and that the only thing left was opium to dull her husband's suffering, which must be unbearable. The doctor was right that Ivan Ilych's physical suffering was terrible, but worse than the physical suffering was the mental anguish, and that was his real torment.
His mental anguish came from this: that night, as he looked at Gerasim's sleepy, kindly face with its high cheekbones, a question suddenly struck him—"What if my whole life has been wrong?"

It struck him that what had seemed completely impossible before—that he had not lived his life as he should have—might in fact be true after all. It struck him that those barely felt urges to push back against what the most highly placed people called good, those faint impulses he had always crushed the instant they appeared, might have been the real thing, and everything else false. And his official work, and the whole structure of his life and his family, and all his social and professional concerns—all of it might have been false. He tried to defend these things to himself, and all at once felt how feeble what he was defending really was. There was nothing to defend.

"But if that's true," he said to himself, "and I'm leaving this life knowing that I've thrown away everything I was given, and that there's no putting it right—then what?" He lay on his back and began to review his life in an entirely new way. In the morning, when he saw first his footman, then his wife, then his daughter, then the doctor, their every word and gesture confirmed the terrible truth that had been revealed to him in the night. In them he saw himself—everything he had lived for—and saw plainly that it was not real at all, but one enormous, terrible fraud that had blotted out both life and death. This realization multiplied his physical suffering tenfold. He groaned and thrashed and tore at his clothes, which seemed to be choking and smothering him. And for that he hated them.

They gave him a large dose of opium and he lost consciousness, but by noon the suffering started again. He drove everyone out of the room and rolled from side to side. His wife came in to him and said:
"Jean, dear, do this for me. It can't do any harm and it often helps. Healthy people do it all the time." He opened his eyes wide.
"What? Take communion? Why? There's no need! And yet..." She began to cry.
"Yes, do it, my dear. I'll send for our priest. He's such a good man."
"Fine. All right," he muttered.

When the priest came and heard his confession, Ivan Ilych softened and seemed to feel some release from his doubts, and so from his suffering, and for a moment a ray of hope appeared. He started thinking again about the vermiform appendix and the chance that it could be set right. He received the sacrament with tears in his eyes.

When they laid him back down afterward, he felt a moment of relief, and again the hope that he might live stirred in him. He started thinking about the operation that had been proposed to him. "To live! I want to live!" he said to himself.
His wife came in to congratulate him on having taken communion, and after the usual conventional words she added:
"You feel better, don't you?"
Without looking at her, he said, "Yes."

Her dress, her figure, the expression on her face, the sound of her voice—all of it told him the same thing: "This is wrong. This is not how it should be. Everything you have lived for, and still live for, is lies and deception that hide life and death from you." And the instant he let that thought in, his hatred came surging back along with the agonizing physical pain, and with the pain came an awareness of the unavoidable end drawing near. To all this was added a new sensation—a grinding, shooting pain and a feeling of being suffocated.
The look on his face as he said that "Yes" was dreadful. Having said it, he stared her straight in the eyes, turned over onto his face with a quickness astonishing in his weak state, and shouted:
"Go away! Go away and leave me alone!"

chapters.title: Chapter 12
paragraphs: From that moment the screaming began, and it went on for three days, so terrible that you could not hear it through two closed doors without being filled with horror. The moment he answered his wife, he understood that he was lost, that there was no turning back, that the end had arrived—the very end—and that his doubts were still unresolved and remained doubts.
"Oh! Oh! Oh!" he cried, in one tone after another. He had started by screaming "I won't!" and went on screaming on that long "O" sound.

For three whole days, during which time no longer existed for him, he fought inside that black sack into which some invisible, unstoppable force kept thrusting him. He fought the way a condemned man fights in the executioner's hands, knowing there is no saving himself. And with every moment he felt that, for all his struggling, he was drawing nearer and nearer to the thing that terrified him. He felt that his torment came from being shoved into that black hole, and even more from his not being able to get all the way into it. What blocked him was his conviction that his life had been a good one. That very justification of his life held him fast, kept him from going forward, and tormented him more than anything else.

Suddenly some force struck him in the chest and the side, making it even harder to breathe, and he dropped through the hole, and there, at the bottom of it, was a light. What happened to him was like the sensation you sometimes get in a railway carriage when you think you're moving backward and you're actually going forward, and then all at once realize which way you're really headed.
"Yes, it was all wrong," he said to himself, "but that doesn't matter. It can be put right. But what is the right thing?" he asked himself, and suddenly went quiet.

This was at the end of the third day, two hours before he died. Just then his schoolboy son had slipped quietly into the room and crept up to the bedside. The dying man was still screaming desperately and flinging his arms about. One of his hands fell on the boy's head, and the boy seized it, pressed it to his lips, and began to cry.

At that very moment Ivan Ilych dropped through and saw the light, and it was made clear to him that his life had not been what it should have been, but that this could still be put right. He asked himself, "What is the right thing?" and went still, listening. Then he felt that someone was kissing his hand. He opened his eyes and looked at his son, and was filled with pity for him. His wife came up to him, and he glanced at her. She was staring at him with her mouth open, the tears still wet on her nose and cheek, a look of despair on her face. He felt pity for her too.

"Yes, I'm making them miserable," he thought. "They're sorry, but it will be better for them once I'm gone." He wanted to say this, but had no strength to get it out. "Besides, why talk? I have to act," he thought. He looked at his wife, gestured toward his son, and said, "Take him away... sorry for him... sorry for you too..." He tried to add, "Forgive me," but what came out was "Forego," and, too weak to correct it, he simply waved his hand, trusting that the One whose understanding mattered would understand.

And suddenly it became clear to him that the thing that had been crushing him and would not let go was now falling away all at once—from two sides, from ten sides, from every side. He was sorry for them; he had to act so as not to hurt them—to set them free and free himself from this suffering. "How good, and how simple!" he thought. "And the pain?" he asked himself. "What's become of it? Where are you, pain?"
He turned his attention to it.
"Yes, here it is. Well, what of it? Let the pain be there."
"And death... where is it?"
He searched for his old, familiar fear of death and could not find it. "Where is it? What death?" There was no fear, because there was no death.
Where death had been, there was light.
"So that's what it is!" he suddenly said aloud. "What joy!"

For him all of this happened in a single instant, and the meaning of that instant did not change afterward. For those at his bedside, his death throes went on for another two hours. Something rattled in his chest; his wasted body twitched; then the gasping and the rattling grew slower and slower.
"It is finished," said someone near him. He heard the words and repeated them in his soul.
"Death is finished," he said to himself. "It is no more."
He drew in a breath, stopped halfway through the sigh, stretched out, and died.
